newsitem.title: USA: Simpson defense expert tells of prolonged struggle.
newsitem.headline: Simpson defense expert tells of prolonged struggle.

text.p: A forensic expert, testifying on videotape in O.J. Simpson's civil trial, said on Thursday that murder victim Ronald Goldman put up a tough struggle against his attacker before succumbing to severe knife wounds.
Looking at pictures of bloodstains with fresh dirt on them, criminalist Henry Lee said, "Mr. Goldman was in an upright position at one point in time and stepped in the blood."

Asked by Robert Baker, Simpson's lead defence attorney, how long he thought the struggle lasted, the Chinese-born expert replied, "I cannot determine the exact time of the struggle, but it was not a very short one. Mr. Goldman did fight a pretty big fight."

Simpson, who was due to take the witness stand for a second round of testimony on Friday, was acquitted by a criminal court jury of the murders of Goldman and Nicole Brown Simpson in October 1995. He is now in civil court battling battling a wrongful death lawsuit brought by the families of the victims.
The former American football star was called by the plaintiffs in in November and is now being called by his own defence team.

His lawyers have told Judge Hiroshi Fujisaki they will wrap up their case on Monday. The rebuttal phase will follow, then closing arguments, with the jury likely to begin deliberations before the end of the month.

Plaintiffs' attorneys contend Simpson killed Goldman quickly between about 10:35 and 10:40 p.m. on the night of June 12, 1994, giving him time to drive from Nicole Brown Simpson's condominium, where the murders took place, back to his mansion two miles (3 km) away and meet a limousine driver at 10:55 p.m.
Simpson's defence wants the jury to believe Goldman struggled with his assailant for a long time, which would not have given Simpson time to commit the murders and still get home when he did.

Looking at a photograph he had never seen before Lee, who is the state of Connecticut's chief criminalist and director of its forensic laboratory, said he was able to detect "seven major drops of blood" on the public sidewalk in front of Nicole Brown Simpson's condominium, suggesting that the killer left by the front and not the back, as the plaintiffs have argued.
Another trail of blood leading away from the condominium was found in an alley at the rear of the building. The murders took place on the private front walkway leading to the condominium.
Lee also said police investigators missed vital evidence at the murder scene and that Los Angeles police criminalists handled evidence while blood was still wet, leading to possible contamination.

In addition, a blood-soaked envelope containing eyeglasses belonging to Nicole Brown Simpson's mother had been folded after the glasses had been removed and while the blood was still wet. Lee said there was a possibility that wet blood could have been transferred to other evidence items in the laboratory, leading to contamination.

The expert also said he discovered a bloody shoeprint at the murder scene which had been missed by investigators and which was clearly not made by the Italian designer Bruno Magli shoes, which left prints leading away from the scene at the rear.

He said the second footprint had a "parallel line" pattern different from the Bruno Magli pattern. In the criminal case Simpson's attorneys suggested the second shoeprint could mean there were two murderers.
